examShortTricks: Trick 1: Purification method picker — sublimation (camphor, benzoic acid), crystallisation (impure sugar), distillation (liquid with b.p. difference), fractional distillation (close b.p.), steam distillation (oils immiscible with water), differential extraction (solubility difference).
Trick 2: Lassaigne's test: fuse with Na → NaCN (N), Na2S (S), NaX (halogen); N + S together → NaSCN — the three conversions are the core answer.
Trick 3: Qualitative N test: Prussian blue Fe4[Fe(CN)6]3; S: violet with sodium nitroprusside or black with lead acetate; halogens: AgNO3 colours (white/cream/pale yellow).
Trick 4: Quantitative C and H: Liebig combustion — %C = (12/44)(mass CO2/mass sample)×100, %H = (2/18)(mass H2O/mass)×100 — two ratios, two answers.
keyPoints: Purification methods: sublimation, crystallisation, distillation, fractional/steam distillation, chromatography.
Lassaigne's test detects N, S and halogens as sodium salts.
C and H estimated by combustion (Liebig's method).
Chromatography separates by differential adsorption/partition.
practiceQuestions: Q. How will you detect nitrogen by Lassaigne's test? (2 marks) — Prussian blue with FeSO4 + FeCl3 in acid.
Q. 0.2 g organic compound gives 0.294 g CO2 — find %C. (2 marks) — 0.294×12/44/0.2 ×100 = 40%.

examShortTricks: Trick 1: Inductive effect: permanent polarisation through σ bonds, dies out by C3–C4 (−I: NO2, X, COOH; +I: alkyl) — 'through sigma, distance-limited' is the definition mark.
Trick 2: Resonance: delocalisation through π bonds/ lone pairs; stability order: resonance structures with full octets and least charge separation dominate.
Trick 3: Hyperconjugation: 'no-bond resonance' — α-C–H σ electrons delocalise into an adjacent p-orbital; more α-H → more stable alkene/carbocation (Saytzeff and Markovnikov both rest on this).
Trick 4: Carbocation stability: benzylic/allylic (resonance) > 3° (hyperconjugation + I) > 2° > 1° > methyl — the ordering question is a favourite.
keyPoints: Inductive effect: electron displacement along σ bonds; permanent, weak, distance-decaying.
Resonance: electron delocalisation over π systems; stabilises molecules.
Hyperconjugation: σ(C–H) donation into an adjacent empty p-orbital.
All three explain stability orders of carbocations, alkenes and substituted benzenes.
practiceQuestions: Q. Arrange CH3+, CH3CH2+, (CH3)3C+ by stability and justify. (2 marks) — tertiary > primary > methyl via +I and hyperconjugation.
Q. Why is propene more stable than ethene? (1 mark) — six α-H give more hyperconjugative structures.

examShortTricks: Trick 1: SN1 vs SN2 in a table — SN1: 2 steps, carbocation, racemisation, favoured by 3° substrates and polar protic solvents; SN2: 1 step, backside attack, inversion, favoured by 1° substrates and polar aprotic solvents.
Trick 2: Electrophilic aromatic substitution mechanism: E+ generation → π-complex → σ-complex (arenium ion) → deprotonation — naming the σ-complex earns the mechanism mark.
Trick 3: Nucleophilic aromatic substitution needs EWG ortho/para to the leaving group (2,4-dinitrochlorobenzene + OH−) — quote the activation requirement.
Trick 4: Rate law evidence: SN1 rate ∝ [RX] only; SN2 rate ∝ [RX][Nu] — kinetics decides the mechanism.
keyPoints: SN1 proceeds via a carbocation; SN2 via a concerted transition state.
Tertiary halides favour SN1; primary favour SN2.
Electrophilic aromatic substitution goes through the arenium (σ) complex.
Substituents direct incoming groups ortho/para (activating) or meta (deactivating).
practiceQuestions: Q. Why does 2-bromo-2-methylpropane hydrolyse by SN1? (2 marks) — stable tertiary carbocation; polar protic solvent stabilises it.
Q. Give the mechanism steps of benzene nitration. (3 marks) — NO2+ formation, σ-complex, loss of H+.

examShortTricks: Trick 1: Three phases: initiation (Cl2 → 2Cl·, light), propagation (Cl· + RH → R· + HCl; R· + Cl2 → RCl + Cl·), termination (radical coupling) — name all three for the mechanism mark.
Trick 2: Anti-Markovnikov addition of HBr in peroxides is a radical chain: Br· adds to the LESS substituted carbon — quote the exception applies to HBr only.
Trick 3: Radical stability: benzylic/allylic > 3° > 2° > 1° — resonance-stabilised radicals dominate selectivity.
Trick 4: Inhibition: BHT/vitamin E donate H to radicals and terminate chains — the antioxidant link.
keyPoints: Free-radical reactions proceed by homolysis under light or peroxides.
Chain: initiation, propagation, termination.
Radical stability follows resonance and substitution.
Anti-Markovnikov HBr addition is radical-mediated.
practiceQuestions: Q. Write the propagation steps for methane chlorination. (2 marks) — Cl· + CH4 → CH3· + HCl; CH3· + Cl2 → CH3Cl + Cl·.
Q. Why is the peroxide effect limited to HBr? (1 mark) — only the HBr chain propagation steps are energetically favourable.

examShortTricks: Trick 1: Oxidising agents ladder: KMnO4 (cold dilute = mild; hot alkaline = strong), K2Cr2O7/H+ (1° alcohol → acid), O3 (cleaves C=C), Cu/573 K (1°→aldehyde, 2°→ketone).
Trick 2: Reducing agents: LiAlH4 (reduces everything incl. acids), NaBH4 (aldehydes/ketones only), H2/Ni (C=C, C≡C), Sn/HCl (NO2 → NH2) — one line each.
Trick 3: Elimination (Saytzeff): alcoholic KOH removes HX; the more substituted alkene predominates; E2 needs anti-periplanar H.
Trick 4: Addition: markovnikov for HX; hydration gives Markovnikov alcohol; hydroboration-oxidation is the anti-Markovnikov hydration route.
keyPoints: Oxidation: alcohols → aldehydes/ketones → acids; cleavage with ozonolysis.
Reduction: LiAlH4 and NaBH4 reduce carbonyls; catalytic hydrogenation reduces multiple bonds.
Elimination: β-elimination with alcoholic KOH; Saytzeff product major.
Addition: Markovnikov orientation for HX and H2O.
practiceQuestions: Q. Which reagent converts CH3CH2OH to CH3CHO without over-oxidation? (1 mark) — PCC / Cu at 573 K.
Q. Predict the major product of 2-bromobutane + alc. KOH. (2 marks) — but-2-ene (Saytzeff).

examShortTricks: Trick 1: Conformation order for ethane: staggered (dihedral 60°, minimum energy) > skew > eclipsed (maximum, 12.5 kJ/mol barrier) — draw Newman projections along the C–C axis.
Trick 2: Butane anti conformer is most stable (methyl groups farthest); gauche next — quote 'anti > gauche > eclipsed'.
Trick 3: Combustion: CnH2n+2 + (3n+1)/2 O2 → n CO2 + (n+1) H2O; incomplete combustion gives CO/soot — the general equation earns the mark.
Trick 4: Halogenation selectivity: 3° > 2° > 1° H (radical stability) — explains major product prediction.
keyPoints: Conformations arise from rotation about the C–C single bond.
Staggered (anti) conformer is the energy minimum; eclipsed the maximum.
Complete combustion gives CO2 and H2O.
Free-radical halogenation favours substitution at the most substituted carbon.
practiceQuestions: Q. Draw the staggered and eclipsed conformations of ethane and say which is more stable. (2 marks) — staggered; minimum repulsion between C–H bonds.
Q. Write the combustion equation for propane. (1 mark) — C3H8 + 5O2 → 3CO2 + 4H2O.

examShortTricks: Trick 1: Geometrical isomerism requires EACH double-bond carbon to carry two DIFFERENT groups — check this condition before assigning cis/trans (1,1-dichloroethene has none).
Trick 2: CIP/E-Z shortcut: higher-priority groups on the same side = Z; opposite = E — use when cis/trans naming fails.
Trick 3: Electrophilic addition mechanism: π bond attacks E+ → more stable carbocation → Nu− attacks — the carbocation choice IS Markovnikov's rule.
Trick 4: Heat of hydrogenation measures stability: more substituted alkene → lower heat → more stable (tetra > tri > di > mono).
keyPoints: Alkenes show geometrical (cis-trans) isomerism about the C=C bond.
Electrophilic addition proceeds via the more stable carbocation (Markovnikov).
Peroxide effect: HBr adds anti-Markovnikov by a radical path.
Stability order: tetrasubstituted > tri > di > monosubstituted alkenes.
practiceQuestions: Q. Why does but-2-ene show geometrical isomerism but but-1-ene does not? (2 marks) — each sp2 carbon of but-2-ene has two different groups; but-1-ene has two H on C1.
Q. Give the product of 2-methylpropene + HBr. (1 mark) — 2-bromo-2-methylpropane (Markovnikov).

examShortTricks: Trick 1: Acidity order: HC≡CH > terminal alkynes > alkenes > alkanes — sp (50% s) > sp² (33%) > sp³ (25%) s-character pulls the electron pair; tests: AgNO3/NH3 white ppt, Cu2Cl2/NH3 red ppt.
Trick 2: Addition sequence: alkyne + X2 → trans-dihaloalkene (anti addition) → tetrahalide; + HX twice → gem-dihalide (Markovnikov both times).
Trick 3: Hydration (H2SO4/HgSO4): terminal alkyne → methyl ketone (Markovnikov enol → keto); only ethyne gives acetaldehyde — the exception to remember.
Trick 4: Polymerisation: 3C2H2 → benzene (red-hot tube); 2C2H2 → vinyl acetylene (CuCl/NH4Cl) — two products, two catalysts.
keyPoints: Terminal alkynes are weak acids and form acetylides with Ag, Cu, Na.
Acidity arises from the high s-character of sp carbon.
Additions occur in two stages; Markovnikov orientation for HX and H2O.
Trimerisation of ethyne gives benzene.
practiceQuestions: Q. How will you distinguish propyne from propene? (2 marks) — propyne gives white ppt with ammoniacal AgNO3.
Q. Product of propyne + H2O (HgSO4/H2SO4)? (2 marks) — propanone (acetone) via enol tautomerisation.

examShortTricks: Trick 1: Aromaticity checklist: cyclic + planar + conjugated + (4n+2) π electrons — test each condition explicitly for full marks.
Trick 2: Directive effects: o,p-directing activators (−OH, −NH2, −CH3 donate electrons); m-directing deactivators (−NO2, −COOH, −X is o,p but deactivating) — halogen's special case is the trap.
Trick 3: Mechanism core: electrophile attacks → σ-complex (arenium ion, resonance-stabilised) → H+ lost restores aromaticity — draw the three steps.
Trick 4: Benzene's extra stability: resonance energy ≈ 150 kJ/mol — explains why substitution beats addition.
keyPoints: Benzene: planar hexagon, 6 delocalised π electrons, Hückel aromatic.
Electrophilic substitution via the arenium ion intermediate.
Activating groups direct ortho/para; deactivating direct meta (except halogens).
Resonance energy makes benzene unusually stable.
practiceQuestions: Q. Why is nitrobenzene meta-directing? (2 marks) — −NO2 withdraws electrons; the σ-complex for o/p attack puts positive charge next to NO2 and is destabilised.
Q. State Hückel's rule. (1 mark) — planar cyclic conjugated systems with (4n+2) π electrons are aromatic.

examShortTricks: Trick 1: Classification test: number of C atoms bonded to the carbinol carbon (1°/2°/3°) — decide BEFORE choosing oxidant: 1° → aldehyde/acid, 2° → ketone, 3° → no oxidation (dehydration instead).
Trick 2: Preparation bank: hydration of alkenes (Markovnikov, H2SO4), hydroboration (anti-Markovnikov), reduction of carbonyls (NaBH4/LiAlH4), Grignard + aldehyde/ketone, alkyl halide + aq. KOH.
Trick 3: b.p. order: 3° < 2° < 1° (branching lowers surface area); alcohols >> alkanes of similar mass (H-bonding) — the two comparison lines.
Trick 4: Lucas test: 3° immediate cloudiness, 2° in minutes, 1° no reaction at room temperature — the identification test to quote.
keyPoints: Alcohols are classified as primary, secondary and tertiary.
Prepared by hydration, hydroboration-oxidation, carbonyl reduction and Grignard synthesis.
Higher b.p. than alkanes due to hydrogen bonding.
Lucas test distinguishes 1°, 2°, 3° alcohols by turbidity speed.
practiceQuestions: Q. How will you distinguish 1°, 2° and 3° alcohols? (2 marks) — Lucas test (ZnCl2/HCl) turbidity: immediate (3°), slow (2°), none (1°).
Q. Why are alcohols soluble in water? (1 mark) — they form hydrogen bonds with water (solubility falls as chain grows).

examShortTricks: Trick 1: Phenol > water > alcohol in acidity: the phenoxide ion is resonance-stabilised while the negative charge on alkoxide is trapped on oxygen — the resonance argument is the mark.
Trick 2: Substituent effect: EWG (NO2) increase acidity (stabilise phenoxide); EDG (CH3) decrease — ortho/para nitrophenols are far more acidic.
Trick 3: Kolbe: phenol → sodium phenoxide + CO2 (125 °C, 5 atm) → salicylic acid; Reimer–Tiemann: CHCl3/NaOH → salicylaldehyde — both give ORTHO products; memorise the two product types.
Trick 4: Bromination: phenol + bromine water → 2,4,6-tribromophenol (white ppt) without a catalyst — the test for phenol.
keyPoints: Phenols are more acidic than alcohols due to phenoxide resonance.
Electron-withdrawing groups increase phenol acidity.
Kolbe reaction gives salicylic acid; Reimer–Tiemann gives salicylaldehyde.
Phenol brominates instantly with bromine water (2,4,6-tribromophenol).
practiceQuestions: Q. Why is phenol more acidic than ethanol? (2 marks) — phenoxide is resonance-stabilised; ethoxide is not.
Q. Give the test to identify phenol. (1 mark) — white precipitate with bromine water.

examShortTricks: Trick 1: Williamson synthesis: R–ONa + R′X → R–O–R′ + NaX — use a PRIMARY halide (secondary/tertiary give elimination); mixed ethers need the alkoxide of the larger group.
Trick 2: Cleavage by HI: with excess HI ethers give 2 R–I; the halide attacks the LESS hindered carbon (SN2) — for aryl alkyl ethers, phenol + R–I (aryl–O bond never breaks).
Trick 3: Low reactivity of ethers: no polarity at C–O for aryl ethers (resonance) — explains why anisole resists cleavage on the aryl side.
Trick 4: Dehydration of alcohols: 2 ROH + H2SO4 (413 K) → ether — intermolecular vs intramolecular (433 K → alkene) temperature control.
keyPoints: Williamson synthesis: alkoxide + primary alkyl halide gives ethers.
Ethers are cleaved by excess HI to alkyl iodides and alcohol/water.
Aryl–oxygen bonds resist cleavage (resonance).
Symmetrical ethers form by acid-catalysed dehydration of alcohols at 413 K.
practiceQuestions: Q. Write the Williamson synthesis of methoxyethane. (2 marks) — C2H5ONa + CH3Br → C2H5OCH3 + NaBr.
Q. Anisole + HI gives? (1 mark) — phenol + CH3I (cleavage at the methyl side).

examShortTricks: Trick 1: Preparation pair: oxidation of 1°/2° alcohols; Rosenmund (acyl chloride → aldehyde, poisoned Pd/BaSO4); acyl chloride + dialkylcadmium → ketone — the selectivity of each reagent is the mark.
Trick 2: Nucleophilic addition order: HCHO > aldehydes > ketones (steric + electronic) — reactivity falls with alkyl substitution.
Trick 3: Identification quartet: 2,4-DNP (orange ppt, both), Tollens (silver mirror, aldehydes only), Fehling (red Cu2O, aliphatic aldehydes), iodoform (methyl ketones/ethanal) — one line each.
Trick 4: Clemmensen (Zn–Hg/HCl) and Wolff–Kishner (N2H4/KOH) both reduce C=O to CH2 — acidic vs basic conditions is the distinction.
keyPoints: Aldehydes and ketones undergo nucleophilic addition at the carbonyl carbon.
Aldehydes are more reactive than ketones (steric and electronic factors).
Tollens and Fehling tests detect aldehydes.
C=O can be reduced to CH2 by Clemmensen or Wolff–Kishner reduction.
practiceQuestions: Q. Distinguish acetaldehyde from acetone by a chemical test. (2 marks) — Tollens: silver mirror with aldehyde only.
Q. Why are ketones less reactive than aldehydes? (1 mark) — two alkyl groups hinder attack and donate electrons, reducing the carbonyl's electrophilicity.

examShortTricks: Trick 1: Acidity order: HCOOH > CH3COOH > substituted... EWG (Cl, NO2) raise acidity by −I; EDG (alkyl) lower it; Cl3CCOOH >> CH3COOH — the inductive argument is the mark.
Trick 2: Higher b.p. than alcohols: cyclic DIMERS via double H-bonding — quote 'dimerisation' for the physical-property mark.
Trick 3: HVZ reaction: X2/red P α-halogenates (CH3COOH → ClCH2COOH) — successive halogenation raises acidity stepwise.
Trick 4: Decarboxylation: soda lime → alkane; NaHCO3 test: brisk effervescence (CO2) — the identification test.
keyPoints: Carboxylic acids are stronger acids than phenols and alcohols (resonance-stabilised carboxylate).
Electron-withdrawing substituents increase acidity.
Form dimers through hydrogen bonding (high b.p.).
React with NaHCO3 with effervescence; decarboxylate with soda lime.
practiceQuestions: Q. Why is ClCH2COOH stronger than CH3COOH? (1 mark) — chlorine's −I effect stabilises the carboxylate anion.
Q. Arrange HCOOH, CH3COOH, ClCH2COOH by acidity. (1 mark) — ClCH2COOH > HCOOH > CH3COOH.

examShortTricks: Trick 1: Aldol needs an α-H: dilute NaOH → β-hydroxy carbonyl → heated → α,β-unsaturated aldehyde/ketone (dehydration); crossed aldol uses two different carbonyls.
Trick 2: Cannizzaro needs NO α-H: conc. NaOH → alcohol + acid salt (disproportionation: one molecule oxidised, one reduced) — 2HCHO + NaOH → CH3OH + HCOONa.
Trick 3: HVZ: carboxylic acid + X2/red P → α-halo acid — the red phosphorus converts the acid to the acyl halide, enabling enolisation.
Trick 4: Discriminator: α-H present → aldol; absent → Cannizzaro — answer the 'which reaction' questions with this single check.
keyPoints: Aldol condensation: α-H carbonyls with dilute base give β-hydroxy aldehydes/ketones, dehydrating to enals/enones.
Cannizzaro: non-enolisable aldehydes disproportionate in concentrated alkali.
HVZ: α-halogenation of acids with X2/red phosphorus.
Crossed aldol gives mixtures unless one partner lacks α-H (Claisen–Schmidt).
practiceQuestions: Q. Which reaction does benzaldehyde undergo with conc. NaOH? (2 marks) — Cannizzaro (no α-H): benzyl alcohol + sodium benzoate.
Q. Write the aldol product of ethanal with dilute NaOH. (2 marks) — 3-hydroxybutanal, dehydrating to but-2-enal.

examShortTricks: Trick 1: Preparation bank: reduction of nitro compounds (Sn/HCl or H2/Pd), ammonolysis of alkyl halides (excess NH3 to stop polyalkylation), Gabriel phthalimide (1° ONLY), Hofmann bromamide (RCONH2 + Br2/KOH → RNH2, one carbon LESS).
Trick 2: Hofmann bromamide's 'one carbon less' is the exam trap — the carbonyl carbon leaves as carbonate; quote it.
Trick 3: Gabriel cannot make aryl amines or 2°/3° amines — the limitation 1-marker.
Trick 4: Classification: 1° (RNH2), 2° (R2NH), 3° (R3N) by N-substitution — count N–C bonds, not chains.
keyPoints: Amines classified as primary, secondary and tertiary by N-substitution.
Nitro compounds reduce to amines with Sn/HCl or catalytic hydrogenation.
Gabriel synthesis gives pure primary aliphatic amines.
Hofmann bromamide degradation gives an amine with one carbon fewer.
practiceQuestions: Q. How will you prepare aniline from nitrobenzene? (1 mark) — reduction with Sn/HCl (or H2/Pd).
Q. Why is excess ammonia used in ammonolysis of alkyl halides? (1 mark) — to suppress further alkylation to secondary/tertiary amines.

examShortTricks: Trick 1: b.p. order: 1° > 2° > 3° (H-bonding availability); amines < alcohols (N less electronegative than O) — two comparison lines.
Trick 2: Solubility falls with chain length; lower amines are water-soluble via H-bonds.

Trick 3: Reactions bank: alkylation/acylation (Hinsberg), carbylamine (1° only, foul smell), nitrous acid (1° → alcohol + N2, 2° → nitrosamine yellow oil, 3° → salt) — the HNO2 test separates all three classes.
Trick 4: Aromatic amines: diazotisation at 0–5 °C with NaNO2/HCl — temperature is the scoring condition.
keyPoints: Boiling points: 1° > 2° > 3° amines; lower than alcohols.
Amines are basic; aryl amines less basic (aniline pKb ≈ 9.4).
HNO2 distinguishes 1°, 2°, 3° amines.
Carbylamine test identifies primary amines.
practiceQuestions: Q. How does HNO2 distinguish the three classes of amines? (3 marks) — 1°: N2 gas + alcohol; 2°: yellow oily nitrosamine; 3°: soluble nitrite salt.
Q. Why do tertiary amines have lower boiling points? (1 mark) — no N–H bonds, no intermolecular hydrogen bonding.

examShortTricks: Trick 1: Gas phase: 3° > 2° > 1° > NH3 (pure +I); aqueous: 2° > 1° > 3° > NH3 for methyl series — the inversion in water (solvation of the cation) is the standard explanation.
Trick 2: Aromatic vs aliphatic: aniline << alkylamines — the lone pair delocalises into the ring (resonance), so it is less available; −NH2 ortho/para donation is the same fact from the ring's view.
Trick 3: Substituent effects on aniline: p-nitroaniline much weaker (−R, −I); p-methoxyaniline stronger (+R) — quote one each.
Trick 4: Solvation argument in full: 1°/2° ammonium ions H-bond strongly with water, stabilising them; 3° lacks N–H, so its cation is poorly solvated — why 3° falls last in water.
keyPoints: Basicity in gas phase: 3° > 2° > 1° > NH3.
In aqueous solution: 2° > 1° > 3° > NH3 (methyl series).
Aniline is far less basic than alkylamines (lone-pair delocalisation).
Electron-withdrawing groups reduce basicity; donating groups increase it.
practiceQuestions: Q. Why is aniline less basic than methylamine? (2 marks) — the lone pair is delocalised into the benzene ring and less available for protonation.
Q. Order of basicity of ethylamines in water? (1 mark) — (C2H5)2NH > C2H5NH2 > (C2H5)3N > NH3.

examShortTricks: Trick 1: Diazotisation: ArNH2 + NaNO2/HCl at 0–5 °C → ArN2+Cl− — keep it COLD; above 5 °C the diazonium salt decomposes.
Trick 2: Sandmeyer (Cu2Cl2/Cu2Br2/CuCN) replaces N2+ by Cl/Br/CN; warm water gives phenol; H3PO2 gives benzene — the N2 group is the best leaving group, hence the whole synthetic toolbox.
Trick 3: Coupling: diazonium + phenol (alkaline, para) or + aniline → azo dyes (–N=N–) — the azo linkage is the colour source.
Trick 4: Hinsberg: benzenesulphonyl chloride — 1° gives N-substituted sulphonamide soluble in alkali; 2° gives insoluble sulphonamide; 3° no reaction — the solubility difference separates the three.
keyPoints: Diazotisation of aromatic 1° amines at 0–5 °C gives diazonium salts.
Diazonium salts undergo Sandmeyer, hydrolysis and reduction replacements.
Coupling with phenols/anilines gives azo dyes.
Hinsberg test distinguishes 1°, 2° and 3° amines by sulphonamide solubility.
practiceQuestions: Q. How is benzenediazonium chloride converted to chlorobenzene? (1 mark) — Sandmeyer: Cu2Cl2/HCl.
Q. Why is diazotisation done below 5 °C? (1 mark) — diazonium salts are unstable and decompose when warm.
Q. What is observed in the Hinsberg test with a secondary amine? (1 mark) — an insoluble N,N-disubstituted sulphonamide.
